slides.say: For an area we need a side and the height to it. So here's the equilateral triangle A B C, and every side is a. From the top vertex we drop an altitude to the base.

The altitude is also the median, so it cuts the base into a over two and a over two. Now look at the half on the right. Its angles are ninety, sixty and thirty, so it's a gold triangle. Its hypotenuse is a, and its short leg, opposite the thirty, is a over two.

slides.say: The height is the long leg, so it's the short leg times root three. a over two, times root three, is a root three over two.

slides.say: You can also get the height with Pythagoras, the same half triangle. The hypotenuse squared, minus the short leg squared. a over two, squared, is a squared over four, because the top and the bottom are both squared.
a squared minus one quarter of a squared is three quarters of a squared. Take the root, and the height is a root three over two. The same height. The gold triangle just gets there faster.

Now the area. A side, times the height to that side, divided by two. The side is a, the height is a root three over two, and we divide by two. a times a is a squared, and dividing by two and then by two again is dividing by four. So the area of every equilateral triangle is a squared times root three, over four.

slides: Why learn it by heart? Because the area of an equilateral triangle comes up a lot on the exam, and we don't want to find the height every time and only then the area.

slides.say: At first the formula looks a bit complicated, but there's an easy way to remember it. Think of a folk dance teacher counting the beat, a-two-three-four, a-two-three-four.
That's the formula. a, squared, root three, over four.
